title: AUDITORY PERCEPTION AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE
authors: Angélique A. Scharine, Kara D. Cave, Tomasz R. Letowski

findings.antecedent: Auditory stimulus presence and basic physical characteristics (sound intensity, frequency, duration)
findings.quote: The human response to the presence of auditory stimulus and its basic physical characteristics of sound intensity, frequency, and duration is called auditory sensation.
However, auditory sensation does not involve sound recognition, which requires a higher level of cognitive processing of the auditory stimuli.

findings.antecedent: Higher level cognitive processing of auditory stimuli
findings.consequent: Auditory perception (conceptual interpretation, association with previous experience, adaptation to environment, expected utility)
findings.quote: This higher level processing forms a conceptual interpretation of the auditory stimulus and is referred to as auditory perception. Auditory perception involves association with previous experience and depends on the adaptation to the environment and expected utility of the observation.

findings.consequent: Auditory perception (sound classification, recognition, identification, reasoning, selection, mental synthesis, concept building)
findings.quote: Depending on the level of cognitive processing, auditory perception may involve processes of sound classification, e.g., on speech and non-speech sounds, sound recognition, or sound identification. More complex cognitive processing also may include acts of reasoning, selection, mental synthesis, and concept building involving auditory stimuli but extends beyond the realm of audition.

findings.antecedent: Auditory stimulus arriving at the auditory system
findings.consequent: Physiologic response (sensation and perception of sound)
findings.quote: The minimum level of stimulation required to evoke a physiologic response from the auditory system is called the threshold of hearing or detection threshold
Normal daily variability of the threshold of hearing can be assumed to be 6 dB or less.

findings.antecedent: Repeated measures of hearing threshold (4000 Hz, supra-aural earphones)
findings.consequent: Average standard deviation in within-subject hearing threshold
findings.quote: Delany (1970) and Robinson (1986) used a Bekesy tracing procedure (Brunt, 1985) and supra-aural earphones to assess within-subject variability of the hearing threshold in otologically normal listeners and both reported an average standard deviation in the order of 5 dB at 4000 Hertz (Hz) for repeated measures of the threshold of hearing on the same person.

findings.antecedent: Repeated measures of hearing threshold (insert earphones ER-4B, ascending method of limits, 1 dB steps)
findings.consequent: Average within-subject standard deviation in hearing threshold
findings.quote: Henry et al. (2001) used insert earphones ER-4B (see Chapter 5, Audio Head Mounted Displays) and the ascending method of limits with 1 dB steps and reported average within subject standard deviations between 1.9 dB and 5.3 dB depending on the stimulus frequency.

findings.antecedent: Listener's familiarity, interest, attention, experience, procedural effects
findings.quote: it is useful to differentiate between the physiological threshold defined by the inherent physiological abilities of the listener and the cognitive threshold limited by the listener's familiarity with the stimuli, interest in and attention to the task, experience with existing set of circumstances, and the numerous procedural effects in eliciting the listener's response (Seashore, 1899; Letowski, 1985).

findings.antecedent: Appropriate amount and type of training
findings.quote: The cognitive thresholds can be made close to the physiological thresholds by an appropriate amount and type of training (Letowski, 1985; Letowski and Amrein, 2005)

findings.consequent: Inter-subject standard deviations in hearing threshold
findings.quote: inter-subject (between-subject) standard deviations ranging from 3 dB to 6 dB were reported for low and middle frequencies in a number of studies (Moller and Pedersen, 2004)

findings.consequent: Inter-subject data variability in hearing threshold
findings.quote: and the inter-subject data variability tends to increase with stimulus frequency.

findings.source: Page 5, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: The audibility of low frequency stimuli improves with increasing frequency at an average rate of about 12 dB/octave

findings.consequent: Audibility of low frequency stimuli (below 500 Hz)
findings.source: Page 5, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: and typically decreases with age, from 20 to 70 years of age, by 10 dB or less for frequencies below 500 Hz (ISO, 2000).

findings.consequent: Audibility of high frequency stimuli (above 8,000 Hz)
findings.source: Page 5, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: The typical changes in the threshold of hearing with age, from 20 to 70 years of age, at frequencies above 8,000 Hz, exceed 60 dB in normally hearing population.

findings.antecedent: Sound energy in the 1.5 to 6 kHz range (most sensitive region 3.0 to 4.0 kHz)
findings.source: Page 5, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: As demonstrated in Figure 11-1, the auditory system is especially sensitive to sound energy in the 1.5 to 6 kHz range with the most sensitive region being in the 3.0 to 4.0 kHz range (Moore, 1997).

findings.antecedent: Poor transmission of low frequency energy by mechanical systems of outer/middle ears AND limited mobility of outer hair cells in low frequency range AND high level of low frequency internal body noise
findings.consequent: Low hearing sensitivity at low frequencies
findings.source: Page 6, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: Low hearing sensitivity at low frequencies is primarily due to poor transmission of low frequency energy by the mechanical systems of the outer and middle ears and limited mobility of the outer hair cells in the low frequency range (Moore, Glasberg and Bear, 1997). The presence of the second mechanism is probably due to the high level of low frequency internal body noise, such as that caused by the blood flow, which normally should not be heard.

findings.antecedent: MAF (minimum audible field) vs. MAP (minimum audible pressure) thresholds
findings.source: Page 6, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: The average difference between both thresholds is in the order of 6 dB to 10 dB and has been sometimes referred to in the literature as the “missing 6 dB.”

findings.consequent: Differences between MAF and MAP thresholds
findings.source: Page 6, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: It should be noted that especially large differences between the MAF and MAP thresholds in the 1.5 to 4 kHz frequency region. This difference is the effect of resonance properties of the ear canal and concha.

findings.antecedent: Occluding the ear canal by an earphone
findings.consequent: Amplification of low frequency physiologic noise (e.g., blood flow noise) AND elevation of MAP threshold at low frequencies
findings.source: Page 7, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: occluding the ear canal by an earphone was reported to cause an amplification of low frequency physiologic noise (e.g., blood flow noise) by the closed cavity of the ear canal and elevation of MAP threshold at low frequencies (Anderson and Whittle, 1971; Block, Killion and Tillman, 2004; Brodgen and Miller, 1947; Killion, 1978).

findings.source: Page 5, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: The binaural thresholds of hearing shown in Figure 11-1 and Table 11-1 are approximately 2 dB lower than the corresponding monaural thresholds if both ears have similar sensitivity (Anderson and Whittle, 1971; Killion, 1978; Moore, 1997).

findings.antecedent: Binaural listening in free sound field (0° incidence, English spondee words)
findings.source: Page 7, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: The normative speech recognition threshold for English spondee (two-syllable) words is 14.5 dB SPL for binaural listening in a free sound field with the sound presented at 0° incidence (American National Standards Institute [ANSI], 2004).

findings.source: Page 7, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: The speech awareness threshold (SAT) is approximately 8 to 9 dB lower (Dobie and van Hemel, 2004; Sammeth et al., 1989).

findings.source: Page 7, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: Auditory thresholds for narrow-band noises have been reported by Garstecki and Bode (1976), Mitrinowicz and Letowski (1966), Sanders and Joey (1970), and others. In all of these studies, the reported thresholds correlated very well with pure tone thresholds and were usually within ±3 dB of each other.
Threshold values vary with frequency and are lowest in the 1 to 4 kHz region, similarly as for the air-conduction threshold.

findings.antecedent: Bone conduction stimulation by impinging sound waves
findings.consequent: Sound intensity needed to cause same sensation as air conduction
findings.source: Page 9, Auditory Perception and Cognitive Performance
findings.quote: In the case of bone conduction stimulation by impinging sound waves, such sound waves need to be 40 to 50 dB more intense than those causing the same sensation though the air conduction pathways.

findings.antecedent: Background noise level (30 to 70 dB SPL range)
findings.quote: According to Gardner (1964), the threshold of discomfort is almost independent of background noise level (in 30 to 70 dB SPL range) and exceeds 80 dB SPL.

It depends on the listener, type of sound (tone, speech, noise band), and frequency content of the sound and varies in 80 to 100 dB SPL range for speech signals (Denenberg and Altshuler, 1976; Dirks and Kamm, 1976; Keith, 1977; Morgan et al., 1979).

findings.consequent: Difference between most comfortable listening level and threshold of discomfort
findings.quote: The typical difference between the most comfortable listening level and threshold of discomfort is about 15 dB for pure tones and speech (Dirks and Kamm, 1976)

findings.consequent: Difference between most comfortable listening level and threshold of discomfort
findings.quote: and about 25 dB for noises (Sammeth, Birman and Hecox, 1989).

The threshold of pain represents the highest level of sound that can be heard without producing a pain. The threshold of pain is practically independent of frequency and equals about 130 to 140 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: Tones of very low frequencies (below 20 Hz) at very high intensity levels (exceeding 115 dB)
findings.consequent: Auditory perception (can be heard by some people)
findings.quote: There are reports indicating that tones of very low frequencies below 20 Hz, called infrasound, can be heard by some people at very high intensity levels exceeding 115 dB (Møller and Pedersen, 2004).

findings.antecedent: Tones of very low frequencies (below 20 Hz) at sufficiently high sound intensity levels
findings.consequent: Physical sensations (not heard but immediately felt causing disorientation, pain, and feeling of pressure on the chest)
findings.quote: In general, however, such tones having sufficiently high sound intensity levels are not heard but immediately felt causing disorientation, pain, and feeling of pressure on the chest (Gavreau, 1966, 1968).

findings.antecedent: Ultrasound stimuli (exceeding 20 kHz) applied through bone conduction
findings.quote: people can hear ultrasound stimuli if they are applied through bone conduction (Lenhardt et al., 1991).
As shown in Figure 11-3, the dynamic range of human hearing extends from approximately -10 dB SPL to 130 dB SPL.
hearing sensitivity, especially in the high frequency region, declines with age (Galton, 1883; Robinson and Dadson, 1957)

mechanism_chain.description: The paper discusses the causal pathway from the physical characteristics of auditory stimuli, through their perceptual processing, to their impact on cognitive resources and subsequent cognitive performance.
